section.title: The ooSQLiteStmt Class
section.para: The ooSQLiteStmt class represents a prepared statement in SQLite. An instance of this object represents a single SQL statement. This object is usually referred to as a prepared statement, a compiled SQL statement or simply as a statement.

The life time of a statement object generally goes like this:
Instantiate a new statement.
Bind values to host parameters using one of the bind methods such as bindText, bindInt, or bindNull.
Execute the SQL by invoking step one or more times. Each time step returns ROW, the values of the current result row can be retrieved with the column methods, such as columnText or columnInt.
Possibly, reset the statement using reset, then go back to step 2. Do this zero or more times.
Release the system resources used by the statement by invoking finalize.

In SQLite, host parameters and result columns are numbered from 0. In ooSQLite, as is normal in Rexx, they are numbered from 1: the first parameter of a statement and the first column of a result row are number 1.

Once a statement has been finalized, or if it was not prepared without error, invoking any method of the statement other than its attributes, finalize, and stmtBusy raises a syntax error, 98.900, with the message The ooSQLite statement is not valid, it has been finalized, or The ooSQLite statement is not valid, it was not prepared without error.

Most of the methods of this class work like an SQLite API with a similar name, and return what that API returns: a result code for the bind methods, step, reset, and finalize, or the value asked for. The result codes are the ooSQLite Result Code constants, which, like all the ooSQLite constants, can be used through the statement object itself, because the class inherits the ooSQLiteConstants mixin class: stmt~ROW is the same as .ooSQLite~ROW.

section.title: new (Class method)
section.para: Instantiates a new ooSQLiteStmt object and prepares the statement SQL to be executed.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
dbConn [required]
The open connection to the database that the statement will be executed on. The connection must not be the destination of a backup in progress.
sql [required]
The SQL statement to be prepared for execution. If sql contains more than one SQL statement, only the first one is prepared, and the rest of the text is ignored.
format [optional]
This argument can be used to specify the default format of the result row(s) coming out of the execution of this statement. This argument sets the recordFormat attribute. If this argument is omitted the recordFormat value of the dbConn argument is used to set the attribute.
If specified, it must be one of the ooSQLite Result Set Format Constants that define how a result set is formatted.
Returns a newly instantiated ooSQLiteStmt object.

A new statement object is always returned, even if the SQL could not be prepared, for instance because of a syntax error or a table that does not exist. The program must check the initCode attribute, which is 0 (OK) if the statement was prepared without error. Otherwise, the lastErrMsg attribute describes the error, the statement is finalized, and it can not be used.
The new statement takes the value of its attribute from the attribute of the connection.

Raises syntax errors when incorrect arguments are detected: when dbConn is not an ooSQLiteConnection object, when the connection is closed or is the destination of a backup in progress, or when format is not a valid format.
The functionality of new is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_prepare_v2 API.

This example prepares a query, displays its result rows, and finalizes the statement:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT id, name FROM foods WHERE type_id = 1 ORDER BY name;") if stmt~initCode <> 0 then do say 'Error preparing the statement:' stmt~lastErrMsg return stmt~initCode end
do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW say stmt~columnInt(1)~right(4) stmt~columnText(2) end
stmt~finalize
/* Output:
1 Bagels 2 Bagels, raisin */

section.title: finalized (Attribute)
section.para: Reflects the finalized state of this statement.

listitem.para: Returns true if this statement has been finalized, otherwise false.
The programmer can not set the value of this attribute. It is set internally by ooSQLite.
A statement is finalized by the finalize method, and also when it is garbage collected. A statement that could not be prepared, that is, one whose initCode is not 0, is finalized from the start.

section.title: initCode (Attribute)
section.para: The initCode attribute reflects the result of preparing the statement when the object was instantiated.

listitem.para: Returns the SQLite result code of preparing the statement in new: 0 (OK) if the statement was prepared without error, otherwise one of the Result Code constants.
The programmer can not set the value of this attribute. It is set internally by ooSQLite, and it never changes.

Because new always returns a statement object, even when the SQL could not be prepared, the program should check this attribute before using the statement. When it is not 0, the lastErrMsg attribute describes the error, and the statement is finalized.

This example tries to prepare a query on a table that does not exist:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT * FROM fooods;") say 'initCode: ' stmt~initCode say 'lastErrMsg: ' stmt~lastErrMsg say 'finalized: ' stmt~finalized
/* Output:
initCode: 1 lastErrMsg: no such table: fooods finalized: 1 */

section.title: lastErrCode (Attribute)
section.para: The lastErrCode attribute reflects the last error code recorded by ooSQLite.

listitem.para: The value of this attribute is the last error code recorded by ooSQLite for this prepared statement.
The Rexx programmer can not set the value of the last error code, it is set internally by ooSQLite.

The last error code attribute is similar to the lastErrMsg attribute. Its value is the last status code recorded by ooSQLite. The lastErrCode and the lastErrMsg attributes are always updated together. The error message is always the message that goes with the error code.

Each of the three major ooSQLite objects, an ooSQLiteConnection, an ooSQLiteStmt, and an ooSQLiteBackup object have a lastErrMsg and a lastErrCode attribute. These attributes all serve the same basic purpose, to hold the last error message and code recorded by ooSQLite.

The attributes are most useful when the invocation of new fails to initialize the object correctly due to an error. The lastErrMsg and lastErrCode attributes are always updated during new. For a statement, they are not updated by any other method: they keep the result of preparing it. After the other methods, the error code and message of the connection, given by its errCode and errMsg methods, describe the error.

section.title: lastErrMsg (Attribute)
section.para: The lastErrMsg attribute reflects the last error message recorded by ooSQLite.

listitem.para: This attribute holds the value of the last error message recorded by ooSQLite for this prepared statement. When there was no error, it is not an error.
The programmer can not set the value of this attribute. It is set internally by ooSQLite.

The last error message attribute is similar to the lastErrCode attribute. Its value is the last status message recorded by ooSQLite. The lastErrCode and the lastErrMsg attributes are always updated together. The error message is always the message that goes with the error code. See lastErrCode for when they are updated.
When the statement could not be prepared, the error message is the one returned by the SQLite sqlite3_errmsg API.

This example initializes a new ooSQLiteStmt object. When the initCode attribute is checked, it is seen that an error ocurred, and the last error code and message are printed to the screen:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, 'SELECT * FROM fooods ORDER BY name;') if stmt~initCode <> 0 then do say 'ooSQLiteStmt initialization error:' stmt~initCode say ' Error code:' stmt~lastErrCode '('stmt~lastErrMsg')' end
/* Output:
ooSQLiteStmt initialization error: 1 Error code: 1 (no such table: fooods) */

section.title: null (Attribute)
section.para: Reflects the representation for the SQL NULL value that is returned by the interpreter, for this statement, for database values that are NULL.

listitem.para: Returns the current object the interpreter uses for this statement for the SQL NULL value. If the programmer has not changed this attribute, its value is the value of the attribute of the database connection this statement is assigned to. Normally this is the .nil object.
Set this attribute to either the .nil object, or some alternative string value. Any other object is converted to its string value.

By default, ooSQLite uses the .nil object to represent the SQL NULL value. columnText returns the .nil object for any value that is SQL NULL. However, by changing the value of the null attribute, the Rexx programmer can change the value the interpreter returns for NULL when this statement is executed. Typically this would be done when the returned values are going to be displayed as text and the programmer would prefer to work with a string directly. Perhaps NULL, or no value.

When a ooSQLiteStmt object is instantiated, the null attribute is assigned the value of the object that is used to instantiate the statement. Changing the attribute of the connection afterwards does not change the attribute of the statement.
Note that this attribute does not affect the value the programmer must use to assign a SQL NULL to the database. The programmer must use bindNull for that.
This attribute is provided by ooSQLite, there is no similar feature provided by SQLite.

This example sets the null attribute of the statement to no price. This allows the application to invoke the left method on the returned value without having to check that the return is the .nil object:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods ORDER BY name;") stmt~null = 'no price' do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW say stmt~columnText(1)~left(20) stmt~columnText(2) end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
Bacon 3.75 Bagels 1.25 Bagels, raisin 1.5 Cheese no price */

section.title: &changed11;recordFormat (Attribute)
section.para: Reflects the default format of a result set for this statement.

listitem.para: Returns the format of this statement, one of the ooSQLite Result Set Format Constants: the format given to new, or the value of the recordFormat attribute of the connection when new was not given one, unless it was changed afterwards.
Set this attribute to one of the ooSQLite Result Set Format Constants. Any other value raises a syntax error.

No method of the ooSQLiteStmt class returns a result set: the values of a statement are retrieved one column at a time. The attribute records the format chosen for the statement; it does not change the format used by the connection, for instance by its exec method.
&changed11;In previous versions, this attribute did not work: getting it returned the value of the initCode attribute, and setting it changed the value of initCode.

This example shows that a new statement takes the format of its connection:
db~recordFormat = .ooSQLite~OO_STEM_OF_STEMS stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT * FROM foods;") say stmt~recordFormat -- 3, the format of the connection stmt~finalize

section.title: bindBlob
section.para: Binds a BLOB value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter. The index of a named parameter can be obtained with bindParameterIndex.
value [required]
The data to bind: a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer object. All the bytes of the data are bound, including any embedded NUL characters.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error: RANGE if index is not the index of a parameter of the statement, MISUSE if the statement has been stepped and not reset.

The data is copied by SQLite, so the object passed as value can be changed after the method returns. What is said here about binding values applies to all the bind methods: values can only be bound before the statement is first stepped, or after it is reset; a bound value stays in place, also after a reset, until another value is bound to the same parameter, or the bindings are cleared with clearBindings; and a parameter that has not been bound is NULL.
Raises a syntax error, 93.900, if value is not a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer.
The functionality of the bindBlob method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_blob API.

This example stores some binary data in the picture column of a row:
picture = 'FFD8FFE0'x || 'not really a JPEG image' stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = ? WHERE name = 'Bacon';") rc = stmt~bindBlob(1, picture) if rc == stmt~OK then rc = stmt~step if rc <> stmt~DONE then say 'Error:' db~errMsg stmt~finalize

section.title: bindDouble
section.para: Binds a floating point value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The number to bind. It is converted to a double precision floating point number.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.
See the remarks of bindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The example of bindNull also uses bindDouble.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a number.
The functionality of the bindDouble method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_double API.

section.title: bindInt
section.para: Binds a 32-bit integer value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The whole number to bind, which must fit in 32 bits: from -2147483648 to 2147483647. Use bindInt64 for larger numbers.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.
See the remarks of bindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The examples of bindNull and reset also use bindInt.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 32 bits.
The functionality of the bindInt method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_int API.

section.title: bindInt64
section.para: Binds a 64-bit integer value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The whole number to bind, which must fit in 64 bits: from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.
See the remarks of bindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 64 bits.
The functionality of the bindInt64 method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_int64 API.

This example stores a number that does not fit in 32 bits:
db~exec("CREATE TABLE counters(name TEXT, value INTEGER);") stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "INSERT INTO counters VALUES('bytes', ?);") stmt~bindInt64(1, 9876543210) stmt~step stmt~finalize

section.title: bindNull
section.para: Binds the SQL NULL value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.

A parameter that has never been bound is already NULL. bindNull is needed to set to NULL a parameter that was bound to another value; clearBindings does it for all the parameters at once. The attribute has no effect on binding: it only changes what columnText returns for NULL values.
The functionality of the bindNull method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_null API.

This example inserts two rows with the same statement. The second one has no price:
sql = "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price) VALUES(?, ?, ?);" stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, sql)
stmt~bindInt(1, 2) stmt~bindText(2, 'Ham') stmt~bindDouble(3, 4.5) stmt~step
stmt~reset stmt~bindInt(1, 3) stmt~bindText(2, 'Brie') stmt~bindNull(3) -- no price yet stmt~step
stmt~finalize

section.title: bindParameterCount
section.para: Returns the number of host parameters in this statement.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
The index of the last host parameter of the statement, or 0 if it has none.

This is the number of parameters when the parameters are written as ?, or as names: :name, @name, or $name. A named parameter that appears more than once in the SQL is a single parameter. When the parameters are numbered explicitly, as in ?NNN, the numbers can leave gaps, and the value returned is the largest number used, not the number of parameters.
The functionality of the bindParameterCount method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_count API.
See the example of bindParameterIndex.

section.title: bindParameterIndex
section.para: Returns the index of the host parameter with the given name.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
name [required]
The name of the parameter, as written in the SQL, including its first character: for the parameter :type, the name is :type, not type. The comparison is case sensitive.
The index of the parameter, which can be used with the bind methods, or 0 if the statement has no parameter with that name.
The functionality of the bindParameterIndex method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_index API.

This example lists the parameters of a statement, binds them by name, and executes it:
sql = "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE type_id = :type AND price < :maxPrice;" stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, sql)
do i = 1 to stmt~bindParameterCount say i stmt~bindParameterName(i) end
stmt~bindInt(stmt~bindParameterIndex(':type'), 1) stmt~bindDouble(stmt~bindParameterIndex(':maxPrice'), 1.4) do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW say stmt~columnText(1) end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
1 :type 2 :maxPrice Bagels */

section.title: bindParameterName
section.para: Returns the name of the host parameter with the given index.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.

The name of the parameter as written in the SQL, including its first character, such as :type. For a parameter written as ?, which has no name, and for an index that is out of range, the empty string is returned. A parameter written as ?NNN has that text as its name.
The functionality of the bindParameterName method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_name API.
See the example of bindParameterIndex.

section.title: bindText
section.para: Binds a text value to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
text [required]
The string to bind. SQLite expects the text to be UTF-8. The text ends at its first NUL character, if it has one: use bindBlob for data that can contain NUL characters.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.
The text is copied by SQLite. See the remarks of bindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The example of bindNull also uses bindText.
The functionality of the bindText method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_text API.

section.title: bindValue
section.para: Binds a value taken from a result column of a statement to a host parameter of this statement. The value keeps its datatype: an integer is bound as an integer, a BLOB as a BLOB, and so on.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
A value returned by columnValue, which is a Pointer object.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.

The value returned by columnValue is only valid while the statement it comes from stays on the same result row: it must be bound before that statement is stepped again, reset, or finalized. Once it is bound, SQLite has its own copy. Passing any other Pointer, or a value that is no longer valid, has unpredictable results, and can crash the interpreter.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a Pointer object.
The functionality of the bindValue method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_value API.

This example copies some rows from one table to another, keeping the datatypes of the values:
db~exec("CREATE TABLE cheap(name TEXT, price REAL);") src = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods WHERE price < 2;") dst = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "INSERT INTO cheap VALUES(?, ?);")
do while src~step == src~ROW dst~bindValue(1, src~columnValue(1)) dst~bindValue(2, src~columnValue(2)) dst~step dst~reset end
src~finalize dst~finalize

section.title: bindZeroBlob
section.para: Binds a BLOB filled with zeros to a host parameter of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
length [required]
The size of the BLOB, in bytes. A negative length is the same as 0.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as bindBlob does.
SQLite does not use memory for the zeros while the statement runs, so this is an efficient way to reserve space for a large BLOB.
The functionality of the bindZeroBlob method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_zeroblob API.

This example sets the picture column of a row to 4096 zero bytes:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = ? WHERE name = 'Cheese';") stmt~bindZeroBlob(1, 4096) stmt~step stmt~finalize

section.title: clearBindings
section.para: Sets all the host parameters of this statement to NULL.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
Returns OK.
reset does not change the values bound to the parameters. Use clearBindings when the next execution of the statement should not use them.
The functionality of the clearBindings method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_clear_bindings API.

In this example, the second row inserted gets NULL for the type and the price:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price) VALUES(?, ?, ?);") stmt~bindInt(1, 2) stmt~bindText(2, 'Sausage') stmt~bindDouble(3, 2.25) stmt~step
stmt~reset stmt~clearBindings -- type_id and price are now NULL stmt~bindText(2, 'Unknown food') stmt~step stmt~finalize

section.title: columnBlob
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row as a BLOB.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

A string with the bytes of the value, including any NUL characters. A value that is not a BLOB is converted: text is returned as is, and a number as its text representation. An empty BLOB, a NULL value, and a column that is out of range return the empty string.

What is said here applies to all the methods that return the value of a column, such as columnBlob, columnInt, or columnText: they return a value of the current result row, so they are meaningful only after step has returned ROW, and until the statement is stepped again, reset, or finalized. If they are invoked at any other time, the result is undefined. SQLite converts the value to the type asked for when the column holds a value of another type.
The attribute does not affect this method: a NULL value is the empty string. Use columnType to tell a NULL value from an empty one.
The functionality of the columnBlob method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_blob API.

This example reads the picture of a row, and displays its size and its bytes in hexadecimal:
db~exec("UPDATE foods SET picture = x'89504E470D0A1A0A' WHERE id = 1;") stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT picture FROM foods WHERE id = 1;") if stmt~step == stmt~ROW then do picture = stmt~columnBlob(1) say stmt~columnBytes(1) picture~length picture~c2x end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
8 8 89504E470D0A1A0A */

section.title: columnBytes
section.para: Returns the size in bytes of the value of a column of the current result row.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
The size of a BLOB, or of the UTF-8 text of any other value: the number 3.9 has 3 bytes. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, have 0 bytes.
See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the columnBytes method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_bytes API.
See the example of columnBlob.

section.title: columnCount
section.para: Returns the number of columns in the result set of this statement.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
The number of columns, or 0 for a statement that returns no data, such as an INSERT or an UPDATE.
The number of columns is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step. Compare with dataCount.
The functionality of the columnCount method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_count API.
See the example of columnName.

section.title: columnDataBaseName
section.para: Returns the name of the database that a result column comes from.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the database: main for the main database, temp for the temporary database, or the name given to an attached database. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step. columnTableName and columnOriginName give the table and the column of the table.
The functionality of the columnDataBaseName method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_database_name API.
See the example of columnName.

section.title: columnDeclType
section.para: Returns the declared type of the table column that a result column comes from.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The type as written in the CREATE TABLE statement, such as INTEGER or TEXT. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, when the column of the table was declared without a type, and when the column is out of range, the empty string is returned.
SQLite is dynamically typed: the declared type does not say what type a value has. Use columnType for the type of a value in the current row.
The functionality of the columnDeclType method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_decltype API.
See the example of columnName.

section.title: &changed11;columnDouble
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row as a floating point number.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The value as a number, with all its precision: the shortest number, of up to 17 significant digits, that is converted back to the same floating point value. Text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.

&changed11;Before ooSQLite 1.1, the number was returned with 9 significant digits only: 3.141592653589793 was returned as 3.14159265. A Rexx program computes with 9 digits unless it sets NUMERIC DIGITS: the number keeps its precision, but an arithmetic operation on it is rounded to the current setting.
See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the columnDouble method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_double API.
See the example of columnType.

section.title: columnIndex
section.para: Returns the number of the result column with the given name.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
columnName [required]
The name of the result column, as returned by columnName: for a column with an AS clause, it is the name given there. The comparison is case insensitive.
The number of the column, 1 for the first column, or 0 if the result set has no column with that name. When several columns have the same name, the number of the first one is returned.
The column names are known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step.
This method is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API.

This example finds the columns it needs by name, so that it does not depend on their order in the query:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT id, name, price FROM foods ORDER BY price DESC;") nameCol = stmt~columnIndex('name') priceCol = stmt~columnIndex('PRICE') do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW say stmt~columnText(nameCol)~left(20) stmt~columnText(priceCol) end stmt~finalize

section.title: columnInt
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row as a 32-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The value as a whole number. A floating point value is truncated, so 3.9 is 3, and text that starts with a number is converted to that number. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.

When the value does not fit in 32 bits, only its lower 32 bits are returned, and the result is not meaningful: use columnInt64 for values that can be that large. See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the columnInt method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_int API.
See the examples of new and reset.

section.title: columnInt64
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row as a 64-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
The value as a whole number, converted as columnInt does. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.
See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the columnInt64 method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_int64 API.

section.title: columnName
section.para: Returns the name of a result column.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the column: for a column with an AS clause, the name given there; otherwise, the name SQLite gives it, which for a column of a table is normally the name of the table column, and for an expression is normally the text of the expression. For a column that is out of range, the string NULL is returned.

The names are known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step. SQLite does not guarantee the name of a column without an AS clause, so a program that depends on the names should give them.
The functionality of the columnName method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_name API.

This example displays, for each column of a query, its name, the column, table and database it comes from, and its declared type. The last column is an expression, so it comes from no table:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT id, name AS food, price, price * 2 FROM foods;") do i = 1 to stmt~columnCount say i stmt~columnName(i)~left(10) stmt~columnOriginName(i)~left(8) - stmt~columnTableName(i)~left(8) stmt~columnDataBaseName(i)~left(6) - stmt~columnDeclType(i) end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
1 id id foods main INTEGER 2 food name foods main TEXT 3 price price foods main REAL 4 price * 2 NULL NULL NULL */

section.title: columnOriginName
section.para: Returns the name of the table column that a result column comes from.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the column in its table, without the alias that an AS clause may give it. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step.
The functionality of the columnOriginName method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_origin_name API.
See the example of columnName.

section.title: columnTableName
section.para: Returns the name of the table that a result column comes from.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the table, without the alias that the query may give it. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this method can be invoked before step.
The functionality of the columnTableName method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_table_name API.
See the example of columnName.

section.title: columnText
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row as a string.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The value as a string: text as is, a number as its text representation, and a BLOB with all its bytes, as columnBlob returns it. For a NULL value, and for a column that is out of range, the value of the attribute is returned, which is the .nil object unless it has been changed.
This is the method used most to retrieve values, because any value can be represented as a string. See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.

The functionality of the columnText method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_text API. For a BLOB, SQLite would return only the bytes before the first NUL character; ooSQLite returns all of them.
See the examples of the attribute and of step.

section.title: columnType
section.para: Returns the datatype of the value of a column of the current result row.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants: INTEGER, FLOAT, TEXT, BLOB, or SQLNULL. A column that is out of range is SQLNULL.

SQLite is dynamically typed: the same column can hold values of different types in different rows, whatever its declared type. Retrieving a value with a method of another type, such as columnText for an integer, can convert the value in place, and then the type returned by this method afterwards is undefined: invoke columnType before retrieving the value. See the remarks of columnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the columnType method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_type API.

This example formats the price of each food according to its type:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods;") stmt~null = 'n/a' do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW select when stmt~columnType(2) == stmt~SQLNULL then price = stmt~columnText(2) when stmt~columnType(2) == stmt~FLOAT then price = stmt~columnDouble(2)~format(, 2) otherwise price = '?' end say stmt~columnText(1)~left(20) price end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
Bagels 1.25 Bagels, raisin 1.50 Bacon 3.75 Cheese n/a */

section.title: columnValue
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row, in the form needed to bind it to a host parameter with bindValue.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
A Pointer object, which points to an SQLite sqlite3_value structure.

The only use of the value returned is to pass it to bindValue, which binds it to a parameter of a statement keeping its datatype. It is only valid while this statement stays on the same result row: see the remarks of bindValue.
The functionality of the columnValue method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_value API. The value is what SQLite calls an unprotected sqlite3_value.
See the example of bindValue.

section.title: dataCount
section.para: Returns the number of columns in the current result row.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.

The number of columns of the current row: the same as columnCount after step has returned ROW, and 0 when there is no current row: before the statement is stepped, after step has returned DONE or an error, and after a reset.
The functionality of the dataCount method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_data_count API.

This example shows the difference between dataCount and columnCount:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT id, name FROM foods;") say stmt~columnCount stmt~dataCount -- 2 0 stmt~step say stmt~columnCount stmt~dataCount -- 2 2 stmt~finalize

section.title: dbHandle
section.para: Returns the database connection of this statement.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
The ooSQLiteConnection object that was used to instantiate the statement.
The functionality of the dbHandle method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_handle API.

This example uses the connection of the statement to find how many rows it deleted:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE price IS NULL;") stmt~step say stmt~dbHandle~changes 'row(s) deleted' stmt~finalize

section.title: finalize
section.para: Deletes the prepared statement and releases the resources it uses.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.

Returns OK if the last execution of the statement had no error, or if it was never executed. If the last step failed, the error code it returned is returned again. In both cases, the statement is finalized.

After a statement is finalized, its finalized attribute is true, and invoking its other methods raises a syntax error. Finalizing a statement that is already finalized is a harmless no-op that returns OK.

All the statements of a connection should be finalized before it is closed: while there is any statement that is not finalized, close returns BUSY and the connection stays open. A statement that is not finalized is finalized when it is garbage collected, but a program can not know when that happens.
The functionality of the finalize method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_finalize API.

This example finalizes a statement that has not been run to completion:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;") stmt~step say stmt~finalize stmt~finalized -- 0 1

section.title: reset
section.para: Resets this statement to its initial state, so that it can be executed again.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.

Returns OK if the last execution of the statement had no error, or if it was never executed. If the last step failed, the error code it returned is returned again. In both cases, the statement is reset.

A statement can be reset at any time, whether it has been run to completion or not. Resetting a statement does not change the values bound to its parameters: use clearBindings for that. After a reset, new values can be bound, and the statement is executed again by stepping it. Reusing a statement in this way is faster than preparing a new one.
The functionality of the reset method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_reset API.

This example executes the same query for three different values of its parameter:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods WHERE type_id = ?;") do type = 1 to 3 stmt~bindInt(1, type) stmt~step say 'type' type':' stmt~columnInt(1) 'food(s)' stmt~reset end stmt~finalize
/* Output:
type 1: 2 food(s) type 2: 1 food(s) type 3: 1 food(s) */

section.title: &added11;sql
section.para: Returns the SQL text of this statement.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
The text of the SQL statement, as it was given to new. When the text given to new held more than one statement, only the first one is returned, because only that one was prepared.
The text does not change when values are bound to the parameters: the parameters are still shown as they were written. The classic interface has the same function in the oosqlSql routine.
The functionality of the sql method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_sql API.

This example displays the text of a statement:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE id = ?;") say stmt~sql -- SELECT name FROM foods WHERE id = ?; stmt~finalize

section.title: step
section.para: Executes this statement, or advances it to its next result row.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.

One of the Result Code constants. The most common ones are:
ROW
A new result row is ready. Its values can be retrieved with the column methods. Invoke step again for the next row.
DONE
The statement has run to completion: there are no more rows, or, for a statement that returns no data, it has been executed. Do not invoke step again before a reset.
BUSY
The database is locked by another connection. The statement can be stepped again later; see the busyTimeOut and busyHandler methods of the connection.
Other codes
An error. The errMsg method of the connection describes it. ooSQLite enables extended result codes for every connection, so the code is often an extended one, such as CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE (2067) for a duplicate value in a UNIQUE column, rather than CONSTRAINT (19); see extendedResultCodes.

A statement that returns data, such as a SELECT, is stepped once for each result row, and once more to get DONE. A statement that returns no data, such as an INSERT, is executed by a single step, which returns DONE on success.
The functionality of the step method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_step API.

This example displays all the rows of a query, and checks that it ended without error:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name FROM foods ORDER BY name;") do forever rc = stmt~step if rc <> stmt~ROW then leave say stmt~columnText(1) end if rc <> stmt~DONE then say 'Error' rc':' db~errMsg stmt~finalize

section.title: stmtBusy
section.para: Tests if this statement has been stepped, but has not run to completion and has not been reset.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
Returns true if step has been invoked at least once, and the statement has neither returned DONE nor been reset. Otherwise, returns false.
This method can also be invoked on a statement that has been finalized; it returns false.
The functionality of the stmtBusy method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_busy API.

This example shows the value of stmtBusy, and of stmtReadonly, while a query is executed:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;") say stmt~stmtReadonly stmt~stmtBusy -- 1 0 stmt~step say stmt~stmtBusy -- 1 stmt~reset say stmt~stmtBusy -- 0 stmt~finalize

section.title: stmtReadonly
section.para: Tests if this statement makes no direct changes to the database.

listitem.para: There are no arguments to this method.
Returns true if the statement does not write to the database, such as a SELECT, and false if it can, such as an INSERT, an UPDATE, or a DELETE.

A statement can be read only and still change the database indirectly, through a user defined function that executes SQL of its own. Transaction control statements, such as BEGIN and COMMIT, are read only, because they make no changes by themselves.
The functionality of the stmtReadonly method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_readonly API.
See the example of stmtBusy.

section.title: &changed11;stmtStatus
section.para: Returns the value of one of the performance counters of this statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
op [required]
The counter to return, one of the Status Parameter (stmt) constants, such as STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP or STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP.
reset [optional]
If true, the counter is set to 0 after its value is returned. The default is false.
The value of the counter. For an op that is not one of the constants, 0 is returned, and nothing is reset.
The counters accumulate over all the executions of the statement, also after a reset, until they are reset with the reset argument. They can help find out whether a query would benefit from an index.
The functionality of the stmtStatus method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_stmt_status API.

This example runs a query and displays some of its counters. There is no index on the price column, so the whole table is scanned, and the result has to be sorted:
stmt = .ooSQLiteStmt~new(db, "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE price > 1 ORDER BY name;") do while stmt~step == stmt~ROW end say 'Full scan steps:' stmt~stmtStatus(stmt~STMTSTATUS_FULLSCAN_STEP) say 'Sorts: ' stmt~stmtStatus(stmt~STMTSTATUS_SORT) say 'VM steps: ' stmt~stmtStatus(stmt~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP, .true) say 'VM steps now: ' stmt~stmtStatus(stmt~STMTSTATUS_VM_STEP) stmt~finalize
/* Output:
Full scan steps: 3 Sorts: 1 VM steps: 47 VM steps now: 0 */
